title: United Airlines Blocks AI Agents From Booking Flights
summary: United Airlines tightens policies to prevent third-party AI agents from booking flights and accessing customer accounts ahead of the 2026 holiday season.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- United Airlines blocks third-party AI agents from booking flights or accessing customer accounts starting November 11, 2026.
- The policy aims to protect customer privacy and prevent unauthorized purchases, as 33% of adults now use AI for travel research.
- United joins other carriers navigating AI adoption, while FTC investigates airline use of personal data in pricing algorithms.


United Airlines announced Wednesday it will block third-party artificial intelligence agents from booking flights and accessing customer accounts, implementing stricter digital platform policies just ahead of the 2026 holiday travel season. The carrier cited privacy concerns and potential safety regulation violations as key drivers behind the policy tightening.


## New Restrictions on AI Booking Tools


United's updated booking, ticketing, and distribution policies specifically target unauthorized personal AI assistants operating on its platforms, whether directly or indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators. The airline warned that sharing login credentials with AI assistants could expose sensitive customer information, lead to unintended purchases or reservation changes, and trigger unauthorized redemption of MileagePlus loyalty miles.


The carrier also noted that automated check-in processes could violate federal safety regulations requiring passengers to personally acknowledge restrictions on hazardous materials in luggage. Officially launched on November 11, 2026, the policy takes effect immediately as the airline prepares for heightened holiday demand.


## Rising AI Adoption in Travel Planning


The move comes as artificial intelligence tools gain significant traction among travelers. According to booking platform Hopper, approximately 33% of adults have used generative AI to research upcoming travel, with expectations for increased adoption this holiday season. The same research revealed domestic airfares for Thanksgiving and Christmas have surged 31% and 23% respectively compared to a year earlier, potentially driving more consumers toward AI-powered fare comparison tools.


These AI travel assistants typically help users:


- Compare flight prices across multiple carriers and booking platforms
- Automatically monitor fare changes and identify optimal booking windows
- Generate personalized itineraries based on budget and preferences
- Handle rebooking and cancellation processes


## Industry-Wide Regulatory Scrutiny


United's policy shift occurs against a backdrop of increasing regulatory attention on airline use of personal data. The Federal Trade Commission recently ordered United, Delta Air Lines, and JetBlue Airways to provide detailed information about their use of customer data in pricing algorithms. This investigation reflects broader concerns that carriers could deploy AI to implement dynamic pricing based on individual willingness to pay.


Delta faced significant backlash in 2025 over plans to expand AI-assisted pricing capabilities, though the airline has consistently denied using the technology to set individualized fares based on personal information. The controversy underscores the tension between AI-driven revenue optimization and consumer privacy expectations.


## Diverging Airline Approaches to AI


Airlines are adopting varying strategies toward artificial intelligence integration. American Airlines maintains strict prohibitions on unauthorized third-party AI tools for flight booking or loyalty account management without written permission, aligning closely with United's new stance.


Southwest Airlines took a different approach in October 2026, introducing a ChatGPT integration that allows travelers to search for flights directly through the AI platform. Delta has developed its own proprietary solution, Delta Concierge, an AI-powered assistant embedded within its mobile app that gives the carrier direct control over the customer experience.


## What This Means


United's decision to block third-party AI agents signals a broader industry reckoning with automated booking technologies. While airlines recognize AI's potential to enhance customer service through first-party applications, they appear increasingly wary of ceding control to external AI assistants that could compromise data security, violate safety protocols, or enable unauthorized transactions. As regulatory scrutiny intensifies and consumer AI adoption accelerates, carriers face mounting pressure to balance technological innovation with robust privacy protections and transparent pricing practices.
